title: Different Ways to Respond
definition: What a person or group does when facing a situation.
content:
Colonial demands affected communities in different ways. Some people worked with new institutions, some changed selected practices, and others opposed demands. A community could also respond differently as conditions changed. Working with an institution does not prove agreement with every rule. Opposing a demand does not mean rejecting every new tool or idea.

Imagine a fictional village report: one family helps repair a meeting place while another asks leaders to change a demand. These actions need separate explanations. Ask what happened, who was involved and what choices were possible. A record of an action may leave the reasons uncertain.

Open all three evidence clues, then choose the explanation they support. You may review the clues or use Explain before answering. We assess the explanation, never your own religion or family identity.
clues: Describe what people did before guessing why.
Ask which demand or change people faced.
One action cannot speak for every family.
task: A village record lists different actions. What should your report do?
Explain each action and the situation it answered
Give every resident one motive
Assume all cooperation meant full agreement
Assume every disagreement meant the same response
reason: Explain each action and the situation it answered. One action cannot speak for every family.

title: Change and Continuity Can Go Together
definition: Changing a way of doing something in response to new conditions.
content:
Adaptation means adjusting to new conditions. Continuity means that something carries on. People may learn a new skill while keeping another practice. We should look for evidence of both change and continuity rather than assume that one new practice replaced a whole culture.

The earlier lesson considered local makers working on religious art. That example helps us ask how existing skills could be used for a new purpose. A commissioned object tells us about work and use; it does not reveal everything its maker believed. Our fictional comparison card shows a maker using a familiar carving skill for a new commission. It is a teaching model, not a surviving workshop record.

Open all three evidence clues, then choose the explanation they support. You may review the clues or use Explain before answering. We assess the explanation, never your own religion or family identity.
clues: A new purpose may change how a skill is used.
An existing skill may continue during change.
An object alone cannot reveal every private belief.
task: A maker uses an existing skill for a new commission. Which idea fits?
Change in purpose can occur alongside continuity in skill
Every older skill disappeared
The object reveals every thought
All communities made the same choice
reason: Change in purpose can occur alongside continuity in skill. An object alone cannot reveal every private belief.

title: A Named Case: Tamblot in Bohol
definition: Action that opposes a demand or authority.
content:
The NCCA CulturEd account describes Tamblot as a babaylan who led an uprising in Bohol in 1621. A babaylan was a spiritual leader in the setting discussed. This case shows that religious change could meet organized opposition. Name the place and period: it is not evidence that all communities reacted in the same way.

The account also reminds us that little is known about much of Tamblots life. Keep a distinction between a documented historical account and details we do not know. We do not need to invent private conversations, make claims about supernatural events, or reenact conflict to learn from this example. Fighting affected people and communities; this learning game awards understanding, not harm.

Open all three evidence clues, then choose the explanation they support. You may review the clues or use Explain before answering. We assess the explanation, never your own religion or family identity.
clues: The account dates the beginning of the uprising to 1621.
A named case cannot describe every community.
task: What does the Tamblot example support?
Some people in Bohol organized opposition in 1621
Every community reacted identically
All details of Tamblots life are known
Violence earns more learning points
reason: Some people in Bohol organized opposition in 1621. A named case cannot describe every community.

title: Living Traditions Need Dated Evidence
definition: Things and knowledge people receive, care for and pass on.
content:
The National Museum Cordillera describes textiles from different groups and recognizes people who keep weaving knowledge alive. Its exhibition includes traditional and contemporary work. This is a useful reminder that Indigenous communities have living histories. They are not people frozen in one time or one shared way of life.

A museum textile can help us ask about a maker, material and date. It cannot automatically prove that every detail existed unchanged during Spanish rule. This mission uses a modern teaching diagram rather than copying a sacred object or claiming to reproduce an authentic pattern. Compare what a source actually dates with the claim you want to make. Continuing knowledge and new materials can belong to the same living tradition.

Open all three evidence clues, then choose the explanation they support. You may review the clues or use Explain before answering. We assess the explanation, never your own religion or family identity.
clues: People pass on knowledge and can also make changes.
Ask when an object was made or collected.
Different groups should not be treated as one identical culture.
task: A modern textile is shown beside a colonial-history claim. What must you check?
Whether dated evidence supports the claim about the earlier period
Whether every feature must be centuries old
Whether all groups use one design
Whether a modern image proves every earlier practice
reason: Whether dated evidence supports the claim about the earlier period. Different groups should not be treated as one identical culture.

title: Build an Explanation with Evidence
definition: Information that helps support or check a claim.
content:
A strong explanation connects a response with evidence and a limit. Try three steps: name the action, give a clue that supports it, and say what the clue does not tell you. Different sources can answer different questions. A dated account may describe an event; an object may help explain work or use. Neither automatically supplies every persons reasons.

In this fictional investigation, one card records work on a new commission and another describes opposition to a demand. You can explain two different actions. You cannot combine them into a claim that all residents agreed, or that every person resisted. Ask whether the source identifies the same people, place and time. If it does not, keep the cases separate. Saying we need more evidence is a useful finding, not a failure.

Open all three evidence clues, then choose the explanation they support. You may review the clues or use Explain before answering. We assess the explanation, never your own religion or family identity.
clues: State the action you are explaining.
Point to a clue that fits that action.
task: Two cards concern different places and actions. What should a report do?
Explain each case with its own support and limits
Merge them into one universal motive
Ignore the dates and places
Invent a conversation linking them
reason: Explain each case with its own support and limits. Say what still needs evidence.

title: Complete Your Community Response Report
definition: Information that helps support or check a claim.
content: You have investigated different responses to colonial change. Review five ideas: people could respond differently; change and continuity could go together; Tamblots case belongs to a named place and period; living heritage needs dated evidence; and explanations need support and limits. Imagine you are preparing a report for another Grade 5 learner. Choose one case and describe the action. Add a supporting clue, then say what you still cannot know. Do not invent private thoughts or treat one community as all communities. You do not need to disclose a belief or act out a conflict. The main quiz checks five topics. Pass with at least three correct to finish this mission and receive its reward once. If you need help, review the linked lesson before targeted practice and a retry. Complete all missions, then pass the chapter challenge to earn the chapter badge.
clues: State the action you are explaining.
Point to a clue that fits that action.
task: Which final report best uses this mission?
Name a response, connect it to evidence and state a limit
Give every community the same motive
Present a modern object as proof of every earlier detail
Earn points by acting out harm
reason: Name the response, support it with evidence and say what remains uncertain.
